sections.title: Why Container Logging Breaks Everything You Knew About Log Files
sections.content:
In traditional VM deployments, applications write log files to disk and log rotation tools manage their lifecycle. In Kubernetes, that model breaks completely. Pods are **ephemeral** — when a pod crashes or gets rescheduled, any log files inside the container vanish instantly. Writing logs to files inside containers is not just inefficient, it is data loss waiting to happen.

Kubernetes establishes a different contract: your application writes to **stdout and stderr**, the kubelet captures those streams to node-level files under `/var/log/containers/`, and a log collector running on each node forwards them to a central store. The application should be completely ignorant of log shipping mechanics. This separation keeps containers portable and makes the logging pipeline consistent across every service in the cluster.

The node-level **DaemonSet pattern** is the standard collection approach: a logging agent like Fluent Bit or Filebeat runs on every node, reads container log files, enriches them with Kubernetes metadata (pod name, namespace, labels), and forwards to Elasticsearch or a cloud logging service. This is fundamentally different from per-application log shipping, and understanding why this architecture exists is what interviewers are looking for.

sections.title: The stdout Contract: How Spring Boot Logs Reach the Collector
sections.content:
The first requirement is that your Spring Boot application writes structured JSON to stdout — not to a file, not to a network socket, just stdout. The kubelet captures the container's stdout stream and writes it to a log file on the node's filesystem. The DaemonSet collector tails that node-level file.

```xml
<!-- logback-spring.xml for Kubernetes -->
<configuration>
  <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
      <includeMdc>true</includeMdc>
    </encoder>
  </appender>
  <root level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE" />
  </root>
</configuration>
```

The `ConsoleAppender` writes to stdout by default. Using `LogstashEncoder` ensures each log line is a complete JSON object that the collector can parse without regex. Do not use file appenders in containers — they compete with the kubelet's stream capture, complicate log rotation, and lose data on pod restart. If you need to preserve logs across container restarts, that is the job of the collector and the central store, not the application.

sections.title: DaemonSet vs Sidecar: Two Collection Patterns and When Each Wins
sections.content:
The **DaemonSet pattern** runs one collector pod per node. Fluent Bit or Filebeat tails all container log files from `/var/log/containers/` on the host, collecting logs from every pod on that node with a single process. The overhead is predictable and shared — one collector process handles all pods, which scales better than alternatives.

```yaml
# Fluent Bit DaemonSet input + Kubernetes filter (simplified)
[INPUT]
    Name              tail
    Path              /var/log/containers/*.log
    Parser            docker
    Tag               kube.*
[FILTER]
    Name              kubernetes
    Match             kube.*
    Kube_URL          https://kubernetes.default.svc:443
    Merge_Log         On    # Promotes JSON fields into the record
[OUTPUT]
    Name              es
    Match             *
    Host              elasticsearch-service
    Index             fluentbit
```

The **sidecar pattern** runs a collector container alongside your application container in the same pod. This is useful when different services need different log processing pipelines, when multi-tenant isolation requires per-pod log routing, or when the application writes to a file that the sidecar tails. The trade-off is resource overhead: every pod gets its own collector process, which adds CPU and memory to every replica. For most Spring Boot deployments, the DaemonSet pattern is the right default.

sections.title: Kubernetes Metadata Enrichment: The Context That Makes Logs Actionable
sections.content:
The most valuable capability of Kubernetes log aggregation is **automatic metadata enrichment**. The Fluent Bit kubernetes filter attaches pod name, namespace, container name, node name, and all pod labels to every log record. This metadata is not available inside the application — only the collector on the node has access to the Kubernetes API.

This enrichment transforms how you investigate incidents. Filter Kibana for `kubernetes.labels.app: order-service AND level: ERROR` and you see errors from all pods of that deployment. During a rolling deployment, you can filter by `kubernetes.labels.version: v2.1.3` to compare logs from the new version against the old. If a canary pod is throwing errors that stable pods are not, the metadata makes this distinction obvious.

The `Merge_Log` setting in Fluent Bit is critical for structured JSON logs. When enabled, it parses the JSON content of each log line and promotes the fields to the top level of the record. Without `Merge_Log`, your application's fields like `traceId` and `orderId` are buried inside a nested `log` string field, making Kibana queries verbose and filtering impractical. With it, those fields are first-class citizens alongside the Kubernetes metadata.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Containers write to stdout; DaemonSet ships logs from node files** — application code never manages log file rotation or paths; stdout is the log destination; the platform handles collection
- **Fluent Bit DaemonSet is resource-efficient for Kubernetes log shipping** — one pod per node; low CPU and memory; ConfigMap-based configuration; forwards to Elasticsearch, CloudWatch, or Cloud Logging
- **Kubernetes filter adds pod/namespace metadata to log entries** — Fluent Bit's Kubernetes enrichment adds `pod_name`, `namespace`, and `node_name` without application code changes; enables filtering by deployment across rolling restarts
- **JSON stdout from Spring Boot enables field-level indexing without grok** — Fluent Bit's JSON parser recognizes structured fields directly; plain-text logs require grok patterns that fail when format changes
- **Multi-line parser required for Java stack traces** — configure Fluentd/Fluent Bit to merge continuation lines (starting with whitespace) with their preceding exception message line; otherwise each stack trace line is a separate unrelated log event

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In Kubernetes, the logging model shifts from application-managed log files to stdout/stderr — which means containers write to the console, the kubelet stores the output as node-local files, and a log shipping agent collects and forwards them to a central store.

**How Kubernetes logging works**
- Each container writes to stdout and stderr; the kubelet stores this as log files on the node under `/var/log/pods/`; `kubectl logs pod-name` reads from these node-local files
- Node-local log files are ephemeral — when a pod is evicted or the node is recycled, the logs are gone; centralized log aggregation must collect and forward logs before pods are replaced

**The DaemonSet log shipping pattern**
- A DaemonSet runs one Fluentd, Fluent Bit, or Filebeat pod per node — which means every log file on every node is shipped to the central log store as pods start and stop
- Fluent Bit is the most resource-efficient option for Kubernetes: low CPU and memory footprint; configures in a ConfigMap that mounts into the DaemonSet pods; forwards to Elasticsearch, Cloud Logging, or CloudWatch

**Structured logs from Spring Boot**
- Configure Spring Boot to output JSON to stdout — each log line is a JSON object; the Fluent Bit parser recognizes JSON and indexes fields without regex grok patterns
- Add Kubernetes metadata to log entries via Fluent Bit's Kubernetes filter: pod name, namespace, container name, and node name are added to every log entry automatically — which means `namespace = "production" AND pod_name =~ "orders-.*"` filters logs from all pods in the orders deployment

**Multi-line log handling**
- Java stack traces span multiple lines — a single exception generates 20-50 log lines; without multi-line configuration in Fluentd/Fluent Bit, each line is indexed as a separate event, making stack traces unreadable
- Configure the multi-line parser to merge lines that start with whitespace (stack trace continuation lines) into one log event with the first line (the exception message) as the event start

questions.question: How do OpenTelemetry, Micrometer, and Spring Cloud Sleuth compare, and how do you choose between them?
questions.title: OpenTelemetry vs Micrometer vs Spring Sleuth — Choosing the Right Library
questions.direct_answer: Micrometer handles metrics, Sleuth (replaced by Micrometer Tracing in Boot 3) handles traces, and OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard that covers metrics, traces, and logs in one SDK. For new Spring Boot 3 projects, use Micrometer Tracing backed by the OTel SDK.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking OpenTelemetry replaces Micrometer for metrics — in Spring Boot 3, Micrometer integrates with OTel rather than being replaced by it.

sections.title: Three Libraries, Three Layers: Why They Complement More Than They Compete
sections.content:
The most common confusion in the Java observability ecosystem is thinking you must choose *one* of these three libraries. In reality, they operate at different layers and are mostly complementary. **Micrometer** is a metrics facade — it gives you counters, timers, and gauges with pluggable backends. **Spring Cloud Sleuth** was the tracing layer for Spring Boot 2, now deprecated. **OpenTelemetry** is the CNCF-backed vendor-neutral standard that covers metrics, traces, and logs in a single SDK.

The landscape has converged significantly since 2022. Micrometer 1.10 added a Tracing API called **Micrometer Tracing**, and Spring Boot 3 uses it as the official tracing solution — backed by either the OpenTelemetry SDK or Brave (Zipkin). This means Micrometer now covers both metrics and tracing under one facade, while OpenTelemetry provides the underlying instrumentation engine. Understanding which layer each library operates at is essential for making the right choice without over-engineering your observability stack.

The common mistake is thinking OpenTelemetry *replaces* Micrometer for metrics in Spring Boot. It does not — Micrometer remains the metrics API, and OTel provides the tracing backend that Micrometer Tracing delegates to.

sections.title: The Landscape at a Glance: Where Each Library Fits
sections.content:
The table clarifies what each library provides and where it applies, so the decision becomes straightforward rather than a source of confusion.

| Feature | OpenTelemetry | Micrometer | Spring Cloud Sleuth |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Signals** | Metrics + Traces + Logs | Metrics (+ Tracing facade in 1.10+) | Traces only |
| **Spring Boot 3 support** | Via Micrometer bridge | Native | Deprecated |
| **Auto-instrumentation** | Java agent (zero-code) | Spring-only auto-config | Spring-only |
| **Vendor neutral** | CNCF standard | Multiple registries | Zipkin/Brave focused |
| **Metric backends** | Prometheus, OTLP, + more | Prometheus, Datadog, + 20 more | N/A |
| **Trace backends** | Zipkin, Jaeger, OTLP | Zipkin, Jaeger (via bridge) | Zipkin |
| **Programming model** | OTel API | Micrometer API | Spring annotation/API |
| **Best for** | New services, non-Spring JVM | Spring Boot metrics | Spring Boot 2 legacy |

The critical distinction is the **auto-instrumentation model**. OpenTelemetry's Java agent instruments bytecode at the JVM level — it can instrument any library in any JVM framework, not just Spring. This makes it the go-to choice for Vert.x, Quarkus, Micronaut, or plain Java services.

Micrometer's auto-configuration is Spring-specific but **deeper within the Spring ecosystem**. It provides rich out-of-the-box metrics for Spring MVC request handling, WebFlux reactive streams, JDBC connection pools, Spring Cache hit rates, and Spring Security authentication events. For Spring Boot services, Micrometer delivers more granular metrics automatically than the OTel agent alone. The OTel agent sees HTTP requests and JDBC queries, but Micrometer sees Spring-specific concepts like `@Timed` annotations and Actuator health indicators.

The layering between them is clean in Spring Boot 3: Micrometer provides the **metric API** (counters, timers, gauges) and Micrometer Tracing provides the **tracing API** (spans, trace context). Under the hood, the tracing API delegates to either the OpenTelemetry SDK or Brave. Your application code never imports an OTel class directly — Micrometer provides the facade.

sections.title: The Decision Tree: Choosing the Right Combination for Your Stack
sections.content:
**Spring Boot 3 service (the recommended default):** Use Micrometer for metrics and Micrometer Tracing with `micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel` for traces. This gives you the Spring ecosystem's rich auto-configuration (HTTP metrics, JDBC metrics, cache metrics) plus OpenTelemetry's vendor-neutral trace export. You get the best of both worlds without managing two separate instrumentation systems.

**Non-Spring JVM services (Vert.x, Quarkus, plain Java):** Use the OpenTelemetry Java agent for zero-code instrumentation across all signals. The agent attaches at JVM startup and instruments HTTP clients, JDBC drivers, and messaging libraries without any dependency changes. This is the most flexible option for polyglot microservices platforms.

**Spring Boot 2 legacy services:** Keep Spring Cloud Sleuth for tracing until you can upgrade to Boot 3. Sleuth's API is similar enough to Micrometer Tracing that the migration is low-risk once you do upgrade.

**Multi-vendor export needs:** When you need to send telemetry to both Prometheus and Datadog, or fan out traces to multiple backends, deploy an **OpenTelemetry Collector**. Your application sends OTLP to the Collector, and the Collector routes to any number of backends. This decouples your application from vendor-specific exporters and lets you change backends without redeploying application code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Micrometer for metrics; Micrometer Tracing (Boot 3) or Sleuth (Boot 2) for traces** — Micrometer handles only metrics; tracing is a separate concern; never mix Sleuth with Spring Boot 3
- **Sleuth is deprecated — Spring Boot 3 uses `micrometer-tracing`** — `micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave` for Zipkin/Jaeger; `micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel` for OpenTelemetry backend; Spring Boot Sleuth artifacts are Boot 2 only
- **OpenTelemetry Java agent instruments without code changes** — `-javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar`; auto-instruments Spring, JDBC, HTTP clients, Kafka; configured via env vars; heavier than Micrometer but more comprehensive
- **OTel Collector as a backend-agnostic pipeline** — Spring Boot sends OTLP to the OTel Collector; the Collector exports to Jaeger, Prometheus, Datadog, or any other backend; switch backends by reconfiguring the Collector, not the application
- **Micrometer + Micrometer Tracing is the Spring-idiomatic choice** — integrates with Spring Boot auto-configuration; application.properties for config; lighter than the OTel agent; the recommended starting point for Spring Boot 3 services

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Micrometer, Spring Cloud Sleuth, and OpenTelemetry operate at different layers — they're partly complementary and partly overlapping in scope. Understanding which handles what prevents duplicate instrumentation and configuration conflicts.

**Micrometer — metrics**
- Micrometer is the metrics facade for Spring Boot — it defines the `Counter`, `Timer`, and `Gauge` instruments and publishes to backends like Prometheus, CloudWatch, and Stackdriver
- Micrometer has no tracing capability; it handles only metrics; in Spring Boot 2.x, Sleuth adds tracing separately; in Spring Boot 3, Micrometer expanded to include tracing via `micrometer-tracing`

**Spring Cloud Sleuth — tracing for Spring Boot 2.x**
- Sleuth auto-instruments HTTP, Kafka, and Spring Data calls and propagates trace context through Spring's infrastructure
- Sleuth is deprecated and not available for Spring Boot 3 — for Spring Boot 3, use `micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave` (Zipkin/Jaeger Brave-format) or `micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel` (OpenTelemetry format)

**OpenTelemetry — the vendor-neutral standard**
- OpenTelemetry is a CNCF standard that defines APIs for traces, metrics, and logs — the goal is one instrumentation API that works with any backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Prometheus, Datadog, Honeycomb) by swapping the exporter
- The OpenTelemetry Java agent auto-instruments Java applications without any code changes — attach `-javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar` and configure the exporter; it instruments Spring, JDBC, HTTP clients, Kafka, and more
- The trade-off: the OTel agent is heavier than Micrometer's lightweight registry approach; configuration is via environment variables rather than Spring's `application.properties`

**In practice for Spring Boot**
- Spring Boot 3: use Micrometer for metrics, `micrometer-tracing` for traces; these integrate with Spring's auto-configuration; use OTel agent when you need vendor-neutral instrumentation across non-Spring components in the same JVM

questions.question: What is the difference between a health check and a readiness check in Spring Boot, and what should you expose on /actuator/health?
questions.title: Health Checks vs Readiness Checks — What to Expose on /actuator/health
questions.direct_answer: Health checks report whether the application is alive (used by process supervisors to decide whether to restart). Readiness checks report whether the application is ready to receive traffic (used by load balancers and Kubernetes to decide whether to send requests). Spring Boot 2.3+ separates these into `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the operational difference between liveness and readiness and the consequences of misconfiguring them.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using the same endpoint for both liveness and readiness, causing a pod to be restarted when it is temporarily overloaded rather than just removed from the load balancer rotation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the startup probe as a third probe type in Kubernetes and how to use it with slow-starting Spring Boot applications to avoid false liveness failures on boot.

sections.title: The Restart Storm That Turns a Database Outage Into a Full Application Outage
sections.content:
The most dangerous misconfiguration in Kubernetes-deployed Spring Boot services is including database connectivity in the **liveness probe**. When the database goes down, the liveness check fails, Kubernetes kills the pod, a new pod starts and also fails the liveness check because the database is still down, Kubernetes kills that pod too — and within minutes, every pod in the deployment is stuck in a restart loop. A database outage that should have been recoverable becomes a full application outage that persists even after the database recovers, because all pods are now in CrashLoopBackOff.

The fix requires understanding that Kubernetes asks **two fundamentally different questions** about your application. Liveness: is this process functioning at all, or should I restart it? Readiness: is this pod able to serve traffic right now, or should I remove it from the load balancer? The consequences of failure are radically different — liveness failure kills the pod, readiness failure just removes it from rotation.

Spring Boot 2.3+ provides separate endpoints for each: `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`. Getting the probe configuration right is one of the most operationally important decisions you make when deploying to Kubernetes.

sections.title: The Two Questions Kubernetes Asks — And Why the Answers Must Be Different
sections.content:
The distinction between liveness and readiness is subtle but has enormous operational consequences. This table captures the key differences.

| Aspect | Liveness Check | Readiness Check |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | Is the app process functioning? | Is the pod ready for traffic? |
| **Failure action** | Kubernetes restarts the pod | Kubernetes removes pod from Service endpoints |
| **Spring Boot endpoint** | `/actuator/health/liveness` | `/actuator/health/readiness` |
| **Should check** | Internal state (deadlock, OOM, corrupted state) | External dependencies (DB, cache, message broker) |
| **Should NOT check** | External dependencies | Internal app state unrelated to serving |
| **Recovery** | Pod restart only | Automatic re-addition when dependency recovers |
| **Wrong config risk** | Restart storm during dependency outage | Traffic sent to unhealthy pods |

The critical rule is: **never put external dependency health in the liveness probe**. Database down should not restart your pod — it should remove the pod from the load balancer. When the database recovers, the readiness check passes again and the pod re-enters rotation automatically. No restart, no reinitialization, no startup cost.

sections.title: Configuring Probes That Protect Instead of Destroy
sections.content:
**Liveness probe** — expose only internal health. The liveness endpoint should return UP as long as the JVM is responsive and not in a broken internal state (deadlocked thread pool, corrupted in-memory data structure). Keep the check cheap and fast — a slow liveness check that depends on network calls can itself cause false restarts under load.

**Readiness probe** — include downstream dependencies. Database connectivity, Redis availability, message broker connection — these belong in readiness. When any dependency is unavailable, the pod is removed from rotation but stays alive. Once the dependency recovers, the pod re-enters automatically.

**Startup probe** — use for slow-starting Spring Boot applications. Applications with Flyway migrations, large dependency graphs, or pre-loaded caches can take 60+ seconds to start. Without a startup probe, the liveness probe runs during startup and kills the pod before it finishes initializing. The startup probe disables the liveness probe until the application reports healthy for the first time.

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/liveness
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/readiness
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 20
  periodSeconds: 5
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /actuator/health/liveness
    port: 8080
  failureThreshold: 30       # 30 × 10s = 5 minutes to start
  periodSeconds: 10
```

The startup probe points at the same liveness endpoint but with a high `failureThreshold`. During startup, Kubernetes checks this probe instead of the liveness probe. Once the startup probe succeeds for the first time, Kubernetes switches to the regular liveness probe. This gives slow-starting applications up to 5 minutes to initialize without being prematurely killed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Liveness failure = container restart; readiness failure = remove from load balancer** — never put transient dependency health in liveness; a dependency outage makes liveness fail, causing a restart loop that doesn't fix the dependency
- **Database health belongs in readiness, not liveness** — database unavailable: readiness fails, traffic stops, pod waits; liveness still passes; database recovers: readiness passes, traffic resumes; no unnecessary restarts
- **`management.health.probes.enabled=true` enables Spring Boot's Liveness and Readiness endpoints** — `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` as separate paths; configure Kubernetes probes to these paths
- **Startup probe for slow Spring Boot initialization** — `startupProbe` allows longer startup (60-120s) before liveness begins checking; without it, Kubernetes kills the pod during ApplicationContext initialization
- **Custom `HealthIndicator` for business-critical dependencies** — downstream service health, message broker connectivity, external API availability; assign to readiness group if the service can't serve traffic without it

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kubernetes uses two distinct health check types for different purposes — liveness checks determine if the process should be restarted; readiness checks determine if the pod should receive traffic. Confusing the two causes the most common Kubernetes availability issues.

**Liveness vs readiness — the key distinction**
- A liveness probe failure causes Kubernetes to restart the container — which means it should only fail if the application is in an unrecoverable state (deadlock, JVM OOM, corrupted state machine); if a transient dependency failure makes the liveness probe fail, Kubernetes restarts the pod, which doesn't fix the dependency and causes a restart loop
- A readiness probe failure removes the pod from the load balancer's backend pool — which means the pod is still running but receives no traffic; it recovers when the dependency becomes available, and Kubernetes adds it back to rotation automatically

**Spring Boot Actuator configuration**
- Spring Boot 2.3+ exposes `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` separately; configure `management.health.probes.enabled=true` to enable them
- Liveness: `LivenessStateHealthIndicator` reports `CORRECT` (healthy) or `BROKEN` (restart needed); database connectivity should NOT be in the liveness group
- Readiness: `ReadinessStateHealthIndicator` plus any custom indicators for dependencies that affect traffic serving ability; database and downstream service health belong here

**Database in the readiness probe**
- Put database connectivity in the readiness probe, not the liveness probe — if the database is temporarily unavailable, the pod should stop receiving traffic (readiness fails), but not restart (liveness should still pass)
- When the database recovers, the readiness probe succeeds and the pod re-enters rotation; restarting the pod doesn't fix a database outage and causes unnecessary restarts

**Custom health indicators**
- `@Component class OrderServiceHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator { public Health health() { ... } }` adds a custom health check that appears in `/actuator/health` and can be assigned to the readiness group

questions.question: How do you design an alerting strategy for Java services using SLOs, SLAs, and error budgets?
questions.title: Alerting Strategy: SLOs, SLAs, and Error Budgets for Java Services
questions.direct_answer: Define SLIs (measurable signals like P99 latency and error rate), set SLOs (internal targets like 99.9% success rate), agree SLAs with customers, and use error budgets — the allowed margin of failure — to decide when to alert and when to stop feature work and focus on reliability.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of SRE reliability concepts and how they translate into concrete Prometheus alert rules for Java services.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Alerting on every error instead of sustained error budget burn rate, leading to alert fatigue.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting (e.g., 5-minute and 1-hour windows) to catch both fast and slow burns before the budget is exhausted.

sections.title: The Alert Fatigue Problem: When Every Error Pages, Nobody Responds
sections.content:
Naive threshold alerting — fire when error rate exceeds 1% for one minute — produces two failure modes. It pages the on-call engineer for every transient blip that resolves itself, training them to ignore alerts. And it misses slow degradation: a steady 0.8% error rate that burns through your reliability budget over two weeks without ever crossing the 1% threshold.

**SLO-based alerting** replaces thresholds with a fundamentally different question: 'are we on track to meet our reliability targets?' The framework starts with **SLIs** (Service Level Indicators) — the specific metrics you measure, like the proportion of non-5xx responses or P99 latency. You set **SLOs** (Service Level Objectives) as internal targets — 99.9% availability over a 30-day rolling window. **SLAs** (Service Level Agreements) are contractual commitments to customers, typically set slightly looser than SLOs to give you a safety margin.

The **error budget** is the allowed margin of failure. For a 99.9% SLO, the error budget is 0.1% of requests over 30 days — roughly 43 minutes of total downtime. Alerts fire based on how fast you are *consuming* that budget, not on whether a single request failed. This eliminates both false positives from transient spikes and false negatives from slow burns.

sections.title: From Indicators to Budgets: Building the SLI → SLO → Alert Chain
sections.content:
For a typical Spring Boot service, the two SLIs that capture user-visible reliability are **availability** (proportion of non-5xx HTTP responses) and **latency** (P99 response time under a threshold). Micrometer's `http_server_requests_seconds` metric provides both signals out of the box.

Set an SLO for each: 99.9% availability and P99 under 500ms over a 30-day rolling window. The error budget for 99.9% availability is 0.1% of requests. On a service handling 1 million requests per day, that is 1,000 failed requests allowed per day — or roughly 30,000 over the full 30-day window.

A **burn rate** measures how fast you are consuming that budget. A burn rate of 1x means you will exhaust the budget exactly at the end of the 30-day window. A burn rate of 14.4x means you will exhaust the entire monthly budget in roughly 2 days. A burn rate of 6x exhausts it in 5 days.

The power of this model is that it naturally separates urgent from non-urgent. A 14.4x burn rate is a fast outage that needs immediate response. A 3x burn rate is a slow leak that should generate a ticket, not a page. A 1x burn rate means you are exactly on budget — no action needed.

sections.title: Multi-Window Burn-Rate Alerting: The Prometheus Rules That Actually Work
sections.content:
The gold standard for SLO-based alerting uses two time windows for each alert severity. A **critical page** fires when the error budget is burning at 14.4x over both a 1-hour window AND a 5-minute window. The short window confirms the issue is happening right now (not a stale signal), while the long window confirms it is sustained (not a momentary blip). A **warning ticket** fires at 6x burn rate over a 6-hour AND 30-minute window — this catches slow degradation that would exhaust the budget before month end.

In Prometheus, implement this with recording rules that pre-compute the availability ratio, and alert rules that combine windows with AND logic.

```yaml
groups:
  - name: order-service-slo
    rules:
      - record: slo:availability:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{
            application="order-service",status!~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{
            application="order-service"}[5m]))

      - alert: HighErrorBurnRate
        expr: slo:availability:ratio_rate5m < (1 - 14.4 * 0.001)
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Error budget burning 14x faster than target"
          runbook: "https://wiki.internal/order-service-slo"

      - alert: HighLatencyP99
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.99,
            rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{
              application="order-service"}[5m])) > 0.5
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
```

The recording rule pre-computes availability so the alert expression stays readable and cheap to evaluate. The burn rate threshold `(1 - 14.4 * 0.001)` means 'availability below 98.56%' — a level that, if sustained, exhausts the monthly error budget in two days. The `runbook` annotation links the alert directly to the investigation playbook, so on-call engineers know what to check without searching a wiki.

When the error budget is depleted, teams use it as a policy trigger: halt feature releases and focus on reliability work until the budget recovers. This turns reliability from an abstract goal into a measurable, negotiable constraint between product velocity and system stability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SLI is the measurement; SLO is the target; SLA is the contract** — engineers manage SLOs; product and legal manage SLAs; SLOs should be tighter than SLAs to leave a recovery buffer before contractual consequences
- **Error budget = (1 - SLO) x total requests** — a 99.9% SLO on 1M requests/month = 1,000 allowed failures; track cumulative failures against the budget; stop feature work when budget is exhausted to prioritize reliability
- **Multi-window burn rate alerting reduces noise** — `burn_rate_1h > 14.4 AND burn_rate_6h > 6` catches both sudden spikes and slow degradation; single-threshold alerting fires on transient blips and misses gradual burns
- **Alert on user impact, not metric thresholds** — "error budget depleting at 3x rate" is more actionable than "5xx count > 50"; the former tells you how severe and urgent; the latter tells you nothing about proportional impact
- **Error budget policy drives engineering decisions** — 100% error budget remaining: ship freely; 50% remaining: slow feature work; 0% remaining: freeze features, focus entirely on reliability; the budget makes the trade-off explicit

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
SLO-based alerting changes the fundamental question from "is a metric above a threshold right now?" to "are we consuming error budget at a rate that will exhaust it before the end of the measurement period?" — which dramatically reduces alert noise while catching real reliability problems earlier.

**SLI, SLO, SLA — the definitions**
- SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the measurement — P99 latency, request success rate, availability; a specific, measurable signal from the service
- SLO (Service Level Objective) is the internal target — "99.9% of requests succeed" or "P99 latency < 300ms over a 30-day rolling window"; the level you're committing to maintain internally
- SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the external contract with consequences — fines, credits, or termination if the SLO is violated; most engineering teams work with SLOs, not SLAs directly

**Error budget — the key concept**
- An SLO of 99.9% allows 0.1% of requests to fail — in a month with 1 million requests, that's 1,000 allowed failures; the error budget is those 1,000 allowed failures
- If 800 failures occur in the first week, you've consumed 80% of the monthly budget in 25% of the time — the burn rate is 3.2x the sustainable rate, and you'll exhaust the budget by end of week 2

**Multi-window burn rate alerting**
- Alert when the burn rate is high over both short and long windows simultaneously — `burn_rate_1h > 14.4 AND burn_rate_6h > 6` triggers when the recent hour is burning fast AND the trend is sustained
- Fast burn (1h window, 14.4x burn rate) alerts on sudden catastrophic failures; slow burn (6h window, 6x) catches gradual degradation; both windows required to avoid false positives from transient spikes

**Implementation in Prometheus**
- `rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])` is the error ratio; compare against the SLO threshold to compute burn rate
- Google's "Alerting on SLOs" chapter in the SRE workbook provides the exact formulas for multi-window alerting
